title: Siren
subtitle: A village seen through frightened eyes
summary: Siren is Sony's PlayStation 2 survival-horror game, first released in Japan on 6 November 2003. Several characters become trapped in Hanuda, a village inhabited by hostile shibito, with their experiences unfolding across an interwoven chronology. The player can borrow another person's or creature's sight, gathering information from a position the controlled character may not safely reach. The ability makes seeing an active part of survival. A route through the village depends on understanding where a threat is looking and what its view reveals about a place that remains dangerous to explore directly.
body: Siren is Sony's PlayStation 2 survival-horror game, first released in Japan on 6 November 2003. Several characters become trapped in Hanuda, a village inhabited by hostile shibito, with their experiences unfolding across an interwoven chronology. The player can borrow another person's or creature's sight, gathering information from a position the controlled character may not safely reach. The ability makes seeing an active part of survival. A route through the village depends on understanding where a threat is looking and what its view reveals about a place that remains dangerous to explore directly.

Sightjacking allows the player to study an enemy's surroundings and movements while the protagonist remains elsewhere. The information can reveal when a path becomes safer or where a useful object lies. It does not remove the risk of acting on that knowledge, because returning to the controlled character means leaving the borrowed viewpoint behind. Objectives connect the cast's separate scenarios, giving one person's action consequences for another part of the story. Progress involves learning both the village and the relationships between events, making attention to another perspective useful in more than one way.

Keiichiro Toyama directed and co-wrote the game after his work on the original Silent Hill, with Naoko Sato contributing to the writing and Hitomi Shimizu composing the music. The European and Australian release used the title Forbidden Siren in March 2004, with North America following in April. Reviews praised the atmosphere and originality while finding the play demanding and sometimes obscure. A sequel and later reimagining continued the world. The original's distinctive fear lies in knowing that seeing through an enemy can help the player survive, while also bringing that enemy's presence uncomfortably close.

A horror director builds another unsettling place
